name: Annie Besant
role: British reformer and Indian National Congress president (1917)
summary: Besant campaigned for women’s political rights and organized with workers in Britain, where she wrote in favor of Fabian socialism. After embracing Theosophy she promoted religious education and campaigned for Indian self-government.

sources.usedFor: Her account of breaking with Gandhi over passive resistance in 1919, the Home Rule movement within the Empire, and the aims she set out for self-government.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Besant argued for training and equipping an Indian army led by Indian officers as part of the security of a self-governing India.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Besant assigned people to the skilled work they did best and argued that even a worker with two trades should have compatible specializations.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Besant defended a legally enforceable written marriage contract to protect children's interests and specify spouses' obligations.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Besant condemned vivisection as torture of sentient creatures and treated their suffering as grounds for rejecting that method of research.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Besant’s vegetarian argument called for abstaining from food that required an animal to be killed, including where killing was distinct from other forms of cruelty.

arbitrator-settles-disputes.rationale: Besant proposed replacing war with international arbitration and wanted a federation working through the League of Nations to make that alternative effective.

automate-paid-work.rationale: Besant called for county farms to maximize output with the least human labor and urged public industry generally to make full use of labor-saving machinery.

basic-income.rationale: Besant’s communal system shared output with workers, children and people incapacitated by age or sickness, and withheld support from an able-bodied adult who refused work.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: The bill Besant advanced required legislative appropriations before drawing Commonwealth funds, with a temporary provision for the transition.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Besant treated the consolidation of capitalism into trusts as the industrial reorganization that made large-scale public ownership feasible.

civil-marriage.rationale: Marriage pamphlet: she proposes a simple public declaration, a written contract of partnership that should be stamped and registered when the law permits, in place of the present legal forms.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: The Case for India: 'Other-Government emasculates a Nation, lowers its character, and lessens its capacity'; Britons must give up the idea that India is a possession and treat her as an equal self-governing partner.

class-collaboration.rationale: The Changing World (1909): liberty will never come 'by hatred of class against class'; she wants co-operation and profit-sharing and says the great change must come from above, not below. Her 1880s Autobiography stressed union of all workers against idlers, so +1.

collective-defense.rationale: Besant argued that every member of the Indo-British Commonwealth should come to the defense of any member attacked from outside, citing India’s wartime support for Britain.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Besant condemned Britain’s use of Indian revenues and military strength for imperial purposes while India’s educational and industrial needs went unmet.

communal-electorates.rationale: The bill Besant advanced expressly rejected communal electorates, making voting territorial even while temporarily retaining certain reserved seats.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Besant argued that government by outsiders diminishes a people’s dignity and denounced India’s subjection to an empire without its consent.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Besant wanted India to frame its own constitution through conventions composed of elected council members with power to co-opt additional participants.

constitutional-jury-trial.rationale: Section 57 of the bill Besant advanced designated jury trial as the ordinary constitutional procedure for violations of Commonwealth law, subject to rules under the Act.

culture-before-state.rationale: Besant built institutions for Indian religious and cultural education to restore national confidence and train Indians for self-government before pursuing Home Rule through her newspapers and the Home Rule League.

death-penalty.rationale: Besant opposed executing convicted murderers and argued that the state should restrain offenders while giving them a chance to reform.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Autobiography, her 1884-85 Socialist writings: 'health, comfort, leisure, culture, plenty for every individual', 'enough for each of work, of leisure, of joy'. Stated as a social ideal, not as a guarantee by the state, so +1.

decide-locally.rationale: Besant proposed giving ward panchayats the local functions that municipalities were too stretched to handle, and building up government from the village or ward through successively wider units.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Besant argued in 1917 that Britain and its allies should fight on until the defeat of autocracy, and urged equal standing for Indians serving in that effort.

democracy-best.rationale: Besant rejected treating voter numbers as decisive regardless of judgment. In her mature Indian constitutional proposals she suggested qualified franchises and extra votes based on competence or service.

direct-action.rationale: Besant pursued Home Rule through a campaign for representative government and opposed the Congress turn to Gandhi’s noncooperation program, continuing to seek reform through negotiations and legislative channels.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: The Commonwealth proposal Besant advanced retained the hereditary Crown and gave the King appointment of the Viceroy.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Besant described a social order in which members contribute according to capacity and receive social support according to need.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Besant argued that a stable constitution should start from social obligations and drew on the Indian ideal of mutual duties instead of treating society as a balance of individual rights.

elective-rulers.rationale: Besant’s Commonwealth proposal vested sovereign authority in the King and his successors and provided for a Viceroy appointed by the Crown.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Besant advocated a lasting defense partnership among the nations of an Indo-British Commonwealth and entertained a close alliance with the United States.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: The Commonwealth bill Besant advanced included fundamental rights and required provincial approval as well as parliamentary action for constitutional amendments.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The bill Besant advanced guaranteed all residents equality before the law and prohibited legal disabilities on grounds of sex.

experts-over-public.rationale: Besant argued in her London lectures that informed judgment should prevail in national councils. In 1922 she proposed additional voting weight for qualifications or exceptional service as a way of giving that principle institutional effect.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Besant argued that Indian people were diminished by being legally deprived of rights, using the right to bear arms as an example even when few would exercise it.

gradual-change.rationale: Besant described the shift to socialism as continuous and set out practical institutional changes that would make further reforms easier.

head-of-state-dissolves-parliament.rationale: After a no-confidence vote under Besant’s Commonwealth proposal, the prime minister could ask the Crown’s representative to dissolve the elected chamber.

humans-entitled-to-use-animals.rationale: Same vegetarianism lecture and her condemnation of vivisection in The Changing World; she rejects both animal food and animal experiments, so she does not hold the entitlement as stated.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Besant argued that workers should receive the full product of their labor and proposed distributing the surplus of communal industries among their workers instead of paying it to owners.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Besant attributed the right of self-rule and self-development to both individuals and nations, and treated the freedom of nations as a collective right in her argument for federation.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Besant argued in The Future of Indian Politics that imposing Britain’s political constitution on India disregarded the distinct history, traditions and social arrangements on which Indian institutions needed to build.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Besant rejected treating ancient revelations as binding on society and argued that many scriptural injunctions should be set aside as unsuitable for present conditions.

limit-guns.rationale: Besant denounced the Arms Act for taking away the right to carry arms and leaving villagers unable to defend themselves.

limit-population.rationale: Besant published and promoted practical means of limiting family size, then after becoming a Theosophist stopped reprinting her own pamphlet and refused to sell its copyright because she no longer endorsed teaching the method.

local-essentials-public.rationale: Besant assigned tramways, gasworks and waterworks to municipal administration.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: Besant rejected successive fixed prison terms for habitual offenders, arguing that release should depend on rehabilitation.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Besant argued that public boards could estimate demand and match supply more efficiently than competing private producers.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Besant praised the constitutional Crown as a common head for a voluntary union of free nations and urged that the autocratic imperial title in India be dropped.

more-religion-public.rationale: In her mature Home Rule advocacy, Besant presented religious education and the participation of temples and religious teachers as important to Indian civic and political life.

municipal-businesses-mixed-economy.rationale: Besant proposed opening municipal farms, workshops and stores while private producers remained in business during the transition.

municipal-property.rationale: Besant assigned the railways, telegraphs and other nationally organized industries to kingdom-wide public boards.

nation-first.rationale: Besant argued that Indian participation in a federation would serve both India and wider interests and called for the combined strength of free nations to be used in the service of the world.

national-self-determination.rationale: Besant called self-rule and self-development the right of every nation. For India, she sought sovereign domestic government within a federation of free states.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Besant’s Indian constitutional plan assigned ward councils responsibility for schools, sanitation and food inspection in addition to ordinary public order.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Besant opposed fiscal arrangements under which British legislators would favor British businesses, citing favoritism by colonial authorities as a burden on Indian merchants and manufacturers.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: The Future of Indian Politics: she broke with Gandhi in 1919 over passive resistance because breaking other, non-tyrannous laws seemed illogical and absurd and would breed lawlessness; she wrote articles on the sanctity of law.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Besant argued that a spouse’s wish to end a mistaken union should suffice without requiring the intimate details or the grounds for divorce to be aired in court.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Besant praised Indian states that made religious instruction part of public schooling and urged education in the religion of each pupil’s parents.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Besant argued that people with wealth and education hold them in trust and owe active service to those whose work made their advantages possible.

one-spouse-at-a-time.rationale: Marriage pamphlet: loyalty of one man to one woman is the highest sexual ideal and monogamy is the result of civilization. She states it as an ideal, not as a legal prohibition, so +1.

parliamentary-road-socialism.rationale: Besant told socialists to persuade voters and win local elections, and explained how councils and the national executive could expand public ownership.

physical-labour-duty.rationale: Besant opposed making everyone do manual labor, arguing that the arts and other intellectual work need time, education and specialization.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Besant favored a federation of self-governing nations linked by a common Crown, and envisaged such federations growing into a world commonwealth.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: After defending birth limitation in The Law of Population, Besant explicitly reconsidered the argument in her autobiography, treating contraception as a temporary palliative for suffering whose deepest causes she no longer considered material.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Besant established the Central Hindu College to teach Indian religion and culture alongside Western subjects and to reverse the estrangement from Indian traditions she attributed to colonial education.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Besant invoked the injunction for rulers to care first for the weak and told modern rulers to make the poor and hungry their concern.

production-for-use.rationale: Besant made the production of general wealth the aim of public industry, in place of production for private profit.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Autobiography, her 1884-85 socialist writings object to huge fortunes accumulated out of the toil of others; she does not state the full claim about profit from owning businesses.

property-fundamental.rationale: Besant supported expropriating corporate capital for public use and giving local councils powers to acquire land.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Besant argued that wealth should be held in stewardship for the common good and used to improve the lives of those whose labor helped create it.

public-ownership.rationale: Besant proposed public ownership of railways, mines and large-scale manufacturing, and municipal ownership of gas and water works.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Besant condemned the use of blasphemy laws to punish disbelief and challenged the distinction they drew between free criticism of Christianity and legally protected doctrine.

racial-franchise.rationale: The Commonwealth proposal used territorial electorates and extended the village franchise to residents who met general age and domicile qualifications, without making one ethnicity a condition for voting.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Besant argued that revelations must ultimately be judged by reason and praised sacred texts for the moral truths that readers could verify.

rehabilitation.rationale: Besant rejected punitive prison labor and escalating sentences, and proposed vocational training and release when a prisoner was ready to live independently.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Besant argued that religions share a divine source and teach common spiritual truths through symbols and forms suited to different peoples.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Besant described the loss of mutual help and trust when rural people moved into competition in the towns and urged the restoration of healthy village life.

sacred-nation.rationale: Besant described a nation as a portion of divine life that unites successive generations and gives its people a distinctive role in the world.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Besant held that purported revelations contain contradictions, interpolations and immoral teachings and must be assessed by reason.

second-chamber.rationale: The Commonwealth bill that Besant advanced specified a Senate alongside the elected Legislative Assembly.

separated-powers.rationale: The preamble in the constitutional bill Besant advanced declares the independence of the legislative, executive and judicial spheres necessary to liberty. She also blamed the combination of executive and judicial functions for making justice inaccessible.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: In her marriage pamphlet Besant denounced a husband’s legal authority over his wife and proposed a written partnership between spouses with mutually specified rights and duties.

single-common-good.rationale: Besant argued that wage decisions should consider the economy as a whole and that both sides should seek the common good over the demands of a particular trade.

small-step-social-reform.rationale: Besant proposed extending the powers of existing county councils and progressively taking over industries already organized as trusts.

socialism-needs-revolutionary-war.rationale: Besant proposed persuading electors, winning council elections and expanding public enterprises in competition with private firms.

socialized-markets.rationale: Besant envisioned publicly owned businesses competing with private firms during the transition to socialism.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: Besant defended the right of ordinary Indians to carry arms, including for protection in the villages.

state-directs-investment.rationale: The Case for India: she hopes the Government help given to munition factories in war will continue to industrial factories in peace, and blames the bureaucracy's laissez-faire for foreign takeover of India's mineral and dye industries.

state-harmful.rationale: Besant made the elected councils and the national executive the organizing authorities in her account of industry under socialism.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: In her mature theosophical lectures Besant praised publicly run schools that taught children their parents’ religion and called for that approach to become the model for national education.

tech-with-ancestral-values.rationale: Besant proposed combining the application of modern science in agriculture, industry and education with institutions grounded in India’s historical traditions, and presented Eastern religion and Western applied science as complementary.

traditional-family.rationale: Besant described lasting monogamy as her highest sexual ideal and held that children needed the influence of both mother and father for healthy development.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: The bill Besant advanced directed the High Courts to apply personal law and custom to such matters as inheritance and private dealings, with the defendant’s law applying when the parties’ laws differed.

unions-good.rationale: Besant helped secure improved pay and the abolition of workplace fines for the Bryant and May matchmakers and served for years as secretary of the union formed in the dispute.

vote-at-sixteen.rationale: Besant’s mature Commonwealth proposal set twenty-one as the minimum voting age at every level.

wife-divorce-without-consent.rationale: Besant argued that a wife should be able to obtain divorce when she no longer wished to remain married and opposed compelling a reluctant spouse to stay.

women-suffrage.rationale: Besant devoted her first public lecture to equal political rights for women and later advanced a bill that explicitly prohibited sex-based disqualifications.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Besant argued that an able-bodied adult offered productive employment by the community should receive no relief if they refused it.

worker-ownership.rationale: Besant assigned ownership of large firms to the public as a whole through bodies answerable to the nation or municipality.

notes: Research covered the Fabian essay on industry and municipal government, the birth-limitation campaign and later reversal, marriage and the franchise, theosophical education and ethics, criminal justice and animal welfare, Indian Home Rule and constitutional design, wartime policy, international arbitration and the proposed Commonwealth. Besant’s religious views changed from secularism to Theosophy. Her mature position is used where she explicitly reconsidered an earlier view, and both phases of her publishing record are used for population limitation.
